title: An AI correction is now a top global credit risk, Fitch says
excerpt: Fitch Ratings has gathered a number of the market’s quieter anxieties into a single sentence, warning that a possible AI market correction is now emerging as one of the biggest credit risks facing the global economy. The judgement comes in the agency’s third-quarter Global Risk Outlook, published this week, and it lands at a moment […]
content_html:
Fitch Ratings has gathered a number of the market’s quieter anxieties into a single sentence, warning that a possible AI market correction is now emerging as one of the biggest credit risks facing the global economy.

The judgement comes in the agency’s third-quarter Global Risk Outlook, published this week, and it lands at a moment when the money flowing into artificial intelligence has grown large enough that a stumble would be felt well beyond the technology sector.

The core of the argument is about entanglement rather than any single company’s balance sheet. Equity markets, corporate bond issuance, and even headline economic growth have all leaned heavily on AI over the past year, so a reassessment of long-run returns would not stay contained.

“The scale of AI investment is such that the exposure of the economy and overall capital market to such a correction is significant,” the agency wrote, adding that the way capital markets and economies have become intertwined with AI has “created a vulnerability for credit.”

The worry has been circulating among policymakers for months, and it echoes the BIS warning that an AI bust could hit credit markets as hard as 2008.

Some of the figures Fitch cites make the concentration concrete. It notes that the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio on the S&P 500 is now close to levels last seen during the late-1990s dotcom boom, and that US corporate bond issuance jumped 26% in the first half of 2026.

Much of that borrowing traces back to a handful of names, since Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX together sold roughly $182bn of investment-grade bonds, a spree that has already pushed Big Tech’s AI debt into European markets.

Because the spending shows no sign of slowing, the exposure keeps building. Capital expenditure at Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft is projected to rise about 75% to some $700bn a year, a pace that is now outrunning the cash those businesses generate.

IT investment alone added 1.4 percentage points to US GDP growth in the first quarter, which is the same intertwining seen from the other direction.

When outlays on that scale are funded increasingly through debt, the question of whether AI revenues arrive on time stops being a purely equity-market problem and becomes a credit one, which is precisely the point.

The strain is not hypothetical. Earlier this month S&P cut Oracle to BBB-, one notch above junk, as its data-centre build burned through cash, and Fitch’s outlook reads as a broader signal that the Oracle downgrade may be less an outlier than an early example. Even so, the agency is careful about scale.

A modest pullback would be absorbed, it argues, though a larger, prolonged correction could carry “wider market, macro and credit effects depending on its scale, duration and contagion.”

Fitch’s caution extends beyond markets to the real economy. It has flagged that AI’s efficiency gains could weaken employment and erode tax bases in developed economies even as the technology lifts productivity, and it has separately pointed to private credit as an area worth watching, while judging that segment unlikely to pose a systemic risk on its own.

Across its recent research the through-line stays consistent, because the upside of AI for corporate credit remains largely incremental and hard to quantify, whereas the downside is increasingly easy to model.

None of this is a forecast that the correction will happen, and Fitch does not claim it is imminent. What the agency is describing is a build-up of exposure, the sense that so much of the market’s recent strength now rests on a single bet paying off.

Uncertain revenues, historically stretched valuations, and record borrowing all sit together, and whether that turns out to be prudence or an underpriced risk depends, as Fitch itself concedes, on future returns that nobody can yet see.

content_html_zh:
惠誉评级将市场上一些较为平静的焦虑集中到一句话中，警告称，人工智能市场可能出现的调整正在成为全球经济面临的最大信用风险之一。

这一判断是在该机构本周发布的第三季度全球风险展望中作出的，而这一判断是在流入人工智能的资金已经增长到足以让科技行业以外的领域感受到挫折的时候做出的。

争论的核心是纠缠，而不是任何一家公司的资产负债表。 过去一年，股票市场、公司债券发行，甚至整体经济增长都严重依赖人工智能，因此对长期回报的重新评估不会受到限制。

该机构写道：“人工智能投资的规模如此之大，以至于经济和整个资本市场面临的这种调整是巨大的。”并补充说，资本市场和经济与人工智能交织在一起的方式“造成了信贷的脆弱性”。

这种担忧已经在政策制定者中流传了几个月，这与国际清算银行的警告相呼应，即人工智能泡沫破灭可能对信贷市场造成像 2008 年一样严重的打击。

惠誉引用的一些数据使集中度变得具体。 报告指出，标准普尔 500 指数的周期性调整市盈率目前接近 20 世纪 90 年代末互联网泡沫时期的水平，美国公司债券发行量在 2026 年上半年猛增 26%。

其中大部分借款可以追溯到少数几个名字，因为亚马逊、Alphabet、Nvidia、Meta、甲骨文和 SpaceX 总共出售了约 1820 亿美元的投资级债券，这一热潮已经将大型科技公司的人工智能债务推向了欧洲市场。

由于支出没有放缓的迹象，风险敞口不断增加。 Alphabet、亚马逊、Meta 和微软的资本支出预计将增长约 75%，达到每年约 7000 亿美元，这一速度目前已经超过了这些企业产生的现金。

仅IT投资一项就为美国第一季度GDP增长贡献了1.4个百分点，从另一个方向看也是如此。

当如此规模的支出越来越多地通过债务融资时，人工智能收入是否按时到位的问题就不再是纯粹的股票市场问题，而是信贷问题，这正是问题所在。

这种压力不是假设的。 本月早些时候，标准普尔将甲骨文的评级下调至 BBB-，比垃圾级高出一级，因为其数据中心建设耗尽了现金，惠誉的前景解读为一个更广泛的信号，表明甲骨文的降级可能不是一个异常情况，而是一个早期的例子。 即便如此，该机构对规模仍持谨慎态度。

报告认为，小幅回调将会被吸收，尽管更大规模、更长时间的回调可能会带来“更广泛的市场、宏观和信贷影响，具体取决于其规模、持续时间和蔓延程度”。

惠誉的谨慎态度不仅限于市场，还涉及实体经济。 它指出，人工智能的效率提升可能会削弱发达经济体的就业并侵蚀税基，即使该技术提高了生产率，它还单独指出私人信贷是一个值得关注的领域，同时判断该领域本身不太可能构成系统性风险。

在其最近的研究中，贯穿始终保持一致，因为人工智能对企业信贷的好处在很大程度上仍然是增量的且难以量化，而坏处却越来越容易建模。

所有这些都不是对将会发生调整的预测，惠誉也没有声称调整即将发生。 该机构所描述的是风险敞口的积累，即市场近期的强势很大程度上依赖于单一押注的回报。

不确定的收入、历史上过高的估值和创纪录的借贷都在一起，正如惠誉自己所承认的那样，这是否是谨慎的做法，还是被低估的风险，取决于目前还没有人看到的未来回报。
